v2 retracts the v1 proof, switches the object to density HJ numbers, is internally inconsistent (E^4 vs E^5) and defers the main argument to a future full version; the bearing on d(n) is the researcher's inference.
Survey whose general n x n draw claim rests on an unidentified reference and conflicts with MathWorld.

why: The statement asks for the least winning dimension d(n) as a function of the width. Cain-Raymond-Källersjö show 7x7x7 is not a first-player win, so d(7) >= 4: that moves a lower bound at one width without fixing d(7), so it is a bound, not a case. I marked it checkable because it is an explicit finite matching certificate with public code, and it uses no AI (Hopcroft-Karp matching). The Mouhib and Conlon-Farnsworth-Robertson preprints give lower bounds on Hales-Jewett colouring numbers, and those bound nothing about the game from below, so they are variants. Bastioni et al. play a different game, so also a variant. Shelah's upper bound on HJ numbers would cap d(n) from above, so I kept it as a bound, but marked it doubtful because of the retraction and version confusion. Before the snapshot, Patashnik 1980 (journal paper plus Thompson's check) settles the first-player win at width 4, dimension 3; with Uiterwijk's 4x4 draw that pins d(4) = 3, so I scored it as a case. No pre-snapshot event settles the whole function.
doubts: Close call between scoring Cain et al. as a case (it settles the X-wins question at width 7, dimension 3) and as a bound (it leaves d(7) undetermined); I chose bound because the statement asks for the value of d(n). Whether Shelah v2 still bounds the classical numbers, and so d(n), is unclear from the record. In the survey, ChatGPT is credited with C programs, but no system is listed in ai.systems and the survey proves nothing, so it gets none.
